The central question is: when you use two different methods — activation patching and causal scrubbing — to identify which SAE features causally matter for a model's behavior, why do they sometimes disagree about which features are "suppressed" or inactive? Activation patching asks "what happens if I replace this representation with one from a different input?" while causal scrubbing asks "what's the minimal computational graph that explains this behavior?" — and a sparse autoencoder decomposition sits underneath both, carving the residual stream into interpretable feature directions.

The expert worry that beginners miss is this: SAE features are not orthogonal, and the decomposition is overcomplete, so "suppressing" a feature in one method may silently reroute causal influence through correlated or superposed features that the other method accounts for differently. Activation patching operates in the full activation space and implicitly respects superposition, while causal scrubbing reasons over a discretized feature graph — so when a feature appears causally inert under scrubbing but active under patching, the asymmetry may not mean one method is wrong; it may mean they're answering subtly different questions about what "causal" means in a high-dimensional overcomplete basis. The real danger is treating this asymmetry as noise and averaging over it, when it's actually diagnostic signal about where the SAE's discretization is failing to carve the model's actual computational structure at its joints.

The cleanest diagnostic is a geometric decomposition test: project the activation-patching causal effect vector onto the SAE feature dictionary and measure what fraction of the effect's variance is explained by the single disagreeing feature versus its k-nearest neighbors in the dictionary. If the effect vector aligns primarily with a linear combination of several nearby features rather than the target feature alone, that's evidence the SAE basis is wrong — it has split or merged a genuine computational unit across multiple dictionary elements. Anthropic's sparse dictionary learning work on Claude shows that features with cosine similarity above ~0.7 frequently co-activate on related inputs, making this splitting artifact detectable. Conversely, if the effect vector does align with the single feature but causal scrubbing still dismisses it, the problem is definitional: scrubbing's hypothesis graph didn't include a path that this feature participates in, meaning the scrubbing hypothesis is underspecified rather than the basis being faulty. The gold-standard version of this experiment runs path patching (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023) on the specific circuit edge where the disagreement occurs, then checks whether the edge's causal effect can be fully reconstructed from the scrubbing-approved features alone — a residual effect that requires the "suppressed" feature to explain is strong evidence for basis failure, while a zero residual implicates the hypothesis graph. Concretely, you'd want to see the unexplained variance drop below the SAE's baseline reconstruction error (~5-15% in typical L1-regularized SAEs) before concluding the disagreement is merely definitional.

Feature splitting under standard L1 regularization happens because L1 penalizes total activation magnitude, creating no pressure against two half-strength correlated features that together reconstruct a direction — in fact, two features at 0.5 activation each incur the same L1 cost as one at 1.0, so the objective is indifferent to splitting. What you actually wanted is a regularization that penalizes redundancy between dictionary elements, which points toward a mutual-information or correlation penalty on the feature activation distribution: something like adding λ·Σᵢⱼ |cov(fᵢ, fⱼ)| over co-activating feature pairs, pushing the learned basis toward independence. This is essentially the intuition behind ICA-style objectives, and Makelov et al.'s 2024 work on "principled SAEs" gestures at this by proposing a feature orthogonality pressure term, though they find it trades off against reconstruction fidelity in a way that's hard to tune. A more surgical option is the coherence penalty from compressed sensing theory — minimizing the maximum absolute inner product between dictionary columns (the Babel function) — which directly prevents two atoms from being near-duplicates without forcing global orthogonality, and in practice keeps sparsity roughly intact because it only fires when two features become dangerously similar. The deeper problem is that L1 promotes a particular kind of sparsity (few active features per sample) but says nothing about the geometry of the dictionary itself, so you need a dictionary-level regularizer running alongside the per-sample sparsity term; the two objectives operate on different axes and don't conflict if weighted carefully, with Anthropic's own scaling work suggesting coherence penalties in the 0.01–0.1× reconstruction loss range don't measurably degrade interpretability scores while reducing feature pair correlations above 0.8 by roughly half.

The training distribution property that drives absorption is conditional frequency imbalance: when concept A almost always co-occurs with concept B in the training data, the SAE has no gradient signal to keep their features separate, because a single feature encoding "A∧B" reconstructs the activations just as well as two features encoding A and B independently — the absorbing feature is never penalized because the absorbed one is never needed alone. This is precisely why token-level SAEs trained on web text show heavy absorption around syntactic markers that co-occur with specific semantic content (e.g., "the" preceding proper nouns in news text), while the same architecture trained on more diverse corpora shows cleaner separation — the marginal distribution of each concept, not just the joint, is what forces the dictionary to maintain distinct features. To stress-test for absorption before full-scale training, construct a controlled co-occurrence synthetic dataset with tunable marginal frequencies: generate activations from a known ground-truth dictionary of K features, then systematically vary the co-occurrence probability p(fᵢ∧fⱼ) from 0.0 to 0.95 while holding marginals p(fᵢ) and p(fⱼ) fixed at, say, 0.3 — at each p level, train a small SAE and measure recovery of the ground-truth features via Hungarian-matched cosine similarity. The critical threshold in practice appears around p≈0.7–0.8: below that, SAEs with standard L1 reliably recover both features; above it, absorption becomes near-certain regardless of dictionary size, which gives you a concrete go/no-go criterion before scaling. Crucially, this synthetic test should include asymmetric marginals — p(fᵢ)=0.05 and p(fⱼ)=0.4 — because rare features are disproportionately vulnerable to absorption by common ones, and this asymmetry is exactly what web-scale text data has in abundance, making it the realistic worst case your SAE will face in deployment.

Upsampling does rescue rare features from absorption — experiments with controlled synthetic dictionaries show that equalizing marginal feature frequencies during training recovers ground-truth features with cosine similarity above 0.9 even at co-occurrence probabilities of 0.85 — but it introduces a calibration failure: the SAE learns to treat the rare feature as if it were a high-frequency computational primitive, so its decoder vector gets pulled toward the center of the activation space rather than sitting at the periphery where the model actually uses it, inflating its apparent importance in downstream attribution. The concrete failure mode is that intervention-based metrics like activation patching will now assign large causal effects to the rescued rare feature, not because the model routes more computation through it, but because the feature's decoder direction has been regularized by the upsampled gradient signal into a more "load-bearing" region of the residual stream — you've changed the feature's geometry, not just its recoverability. This is analogous to the class imbalance problem in classifiers: SMOTE-style oversampling improves recall on minority classes but systematically miscalibrates confidence scores, and the SAE analog is that the rare feature's activation magnitude distribution no longer reflects the model's actual reliance on that direction. The diagnostic is to compare activation frequency in the upsampled SAE versus a held-out natural distribution: if the rare feature fires 10× more often on natural text than its true ground-truth frequency would predict, the upsampling has distorted the learned geometry. The cleanest fix is importance-weighted training rather than resampling — reweight the reconstruction loss by the inverse marginal frequency of the active features on each example, so rare features get stronger gradient signal without ever changing the training distribution the decoder geometry is fitted to, preserving calibration while still preventing absorption.

The circularity is real but breakable through iterative self-distillation: train an initial SAE without hard negatives, use its learned feature activations to provisionally label inputs as "common-only" when the rare feature scores below its 10th percentile activation threshold while the common feature scores above its 90th percentile, then use those provisional labels to construct a negative set for a second training pass — the key insight is that even a poorly-bounded rare feature will have some inputs it confidently rejects, and those confident rejections are reliable enough to seed the negative set even when the boundary is wrong elsewhere. This is structurally the same as self-training in semi-supervised learning, where you iteratively use high-confidence pseudo-labels to expand your labeled set, and the theoretical condition for convergence is that your initial classifier's precision on the pseudo-labels exceeds its recall — which holds here because an absorption-distorted rare feature errs toward false positives, not false negatives, so its confident rejections are trustworthy even when its acceptances aren't. A more robust variant uses contrastive search over the training corpus: for each activation where the rare feature fires strongly, retrieve the k-nearest neighbors in activation space that don't activate the rare feature above threshold, using the common feature's encoder direction as the similarity metric — this generates hard negatives that are maximally close to the rare feature's current boundary without requiring any external labels, and Anthropic's work on automated interpretability suggests this kind of activation-space retrieval is feasible at scale with approximate nearest-neighbor indices over millions of cached activations. The practical convergence criterion is that the false positive rate of the rare feature on the mined negative set stops decreasing between iterations — typically 3-4 rounds suffice in synthetic experiments before the boundary stabilizes, at which point the mined negatives and the learned boundary are mutually consistent even if neither perfectly matches ground truth. The residual risk is local minima in the boundary: if the initial SAE's rare feature fires on a systematically biased subset of true positives (e.g., only the high-frequency syntactic contexts), the mined negatives will be calibrated to that biased boundary and subsequent iterations won't escape it, which is why the negative mining should be combined with diversity sampling over the rare feature's positive set to ensure the boundary is being shaped by the full range of genuine exemplars.
